title: Largest number from a list of integers (custom comparator: compare `a+b` vs `b+a`).
shortTitle: Largest Number From a List of Integers: Custom Comparator a+b vs b+a
keyPoints: Sort by comparing the string concatenation a+b against b+a; put the bigger concatenation first
Numeric sorting is wrong: 9 must come before 30 because 930 beats 309
Both concatenations have equal length, so string comparison is safe and avoids numeric overflow
The comparator defines a transitive total order, which is what makes the greedy sort provably optimal
The all-zeros edge case must be handled: if the largest piece is 0, return the single string 0
Runs in O(n log n) time for the sort over n number strings

s1_definition.oneliner: Sort by comparing the string a+b against b+a and put the bigger concatenation first.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Largest Number** – arrange a list of non-negative integers so their concatenation forms the biggest possible number.
- **Custom comparator** – for any two numbers a and b, compare the string a+b against b+a; the one producing the larger string comes first.
- **Equal-length trick** – both concatenations have identical length, so lexicographic string comparison equals numeric comparison, avoiding overflow.
- **Transitivity** – the a+b vs b+a relation is transitive, making it a valid total order for a standard sort.
- **All-zeros guard** – if the input is all zeros, return the single string "0" instead of "000".
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to stitch a set of branch codes into the single largest possible identifier for a priority label. The surprising part is you cannot just sort numerically: 9 should come before 30 because 930 beats 309. For any two codes, try gluing them both ways and keep the order that produces the bigger glued string.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Largest Number problem arranges non-negative integers so their concatenation is the biggest possible number, and the key insight is that numeric sorting is wrong. The number 3 must come before 30 because 330 beats 303, even though 3 is numerically smaller. What matters is which arrangement produces the larger concatenated string.

I define a custom comparator that, for any two numbers, compares the string a+b against b+a. Because both concatenations have the same length, comparing them as strings is the same as comparing them as numbers, which avoids overflow from building enormous numeric values. I sort all the numbers with this comparator and join them.

The correctness rests on the comparator being a consistent total order. The a+b vs b+a relation is transitive, which lets a standard sort produce the globally optimal arrangement. The edge case I always handle is all zeros: if the largest piece after sorting is zero, I return the single string "0" instead of "000".

At the National Bank of India, I used this to assemble numeric branch codes into the largest concatenated identifier for batch priority keys. Explaining why numeric sorting fails, the equal-length string comparison that avoids overflow, the transitivity that justifies the greedy sort, and the all-zeros guard shows the interviewer that I understand both the trick and why it is provably correct.

Remember one sentence: compare the string a+b against b+a for every pair, sort by the larger concatenation, and the greedy result is the globally largest number.
